summary: This document recommends using TLS to protect email between a user's client and the mail submission or access server. It treats TLS from the start of connection as preferred over cleartext plus upgrade, and updates several earlier RFCs for POP3, IMAP and submission.

eli5.summary: Sending mail unprotected is like sending postcards. This says to always use a sealed envelope when your mail app talks to the server.

questions: should email clients use implicit tls
is starttls still recommended for email
subtitle: Why mail clients and servers should use TLS from the first byte, and what that means for ports, DNS and certificates.

tldr.problem: Email clients and servers often support TLS but do not use it in ways that protect users, leaving passwords and messages exposed in cleartext.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends TLS 1.2 or later for all traffic between mail clients and submission or access servers, with Implicit TLS on dedicated ports preferred over STARTTLS, and deprecation of cleartext.
tldr.outcome: It adds Implicit TLS as the recommended way to use POP, IMAP and message submission. It was updated by a later RFC, 8997.

Default minimum for new accounts
facts.value: TLS 1.1 or greater, with certificate validation

today: RFC 8314 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8997. It has not been obsoleted. It updates RFCs 1939, 2595, 3501, 5068, 6186 and 6409.

sections.title: Cleartext Email Access Is Obsolete
sections.content:
Software for IMAP, POP and SMTP Submission usually supports TLS but often does not use it in a way that maximizes confidentiality. RFC 8314 gives current recommendations for traffic between a Mail User Agent (MUA, the mail client) and a Mail Access Server or Mail Submission Server.

In brief: use TLS 1.2 or greater for all such traffic, have MUAs and Mail Service Providers (MSPs) discourage and then deprecate cleartext as soon as practicable, and connect with Implicit TLS in preference to using STARTTLS on a cleartext port.

The memo does not cover TLS for SMTP message relay between servers, and it is not a substitute for end-to-end email encryption.
sections.eli5: Reading and sending your mail should always happen in a sealed envelope, not on an open postcard.

sections.title: Implicit TLS on Dedicated Ports
sections.content:
With Implicit TLS, a TLS handshake begins immediately when a TCP connection opens on a port used only for TLS. This contrasts with STARTTLS, where a client opens a cleartext session and then asks to upgrade. The RFC says Implicit TLS has been deployed more successfully.

  • POP: service pop3s, default port 995.
  • IMAP: service imaps, default port 993. A server MAY greet with PREAUTH if it accepts a client certificate.
  • SMTP Submission: service submissions, default port 465.

Clients MUST implement certificate validation as described in RFC 7817. Because STARTTLS on port 587 is widely deployed for submission, clients and servers SHOULD implement both it and Implicit TLS on port 465 for a transition period of several years. Done correctly, the two have no significant difference in security properties. On closing, either side SHOULD exchange TLS close alerts before TCP termination.
sections.eli5: It is the difference between knocking on a door and then asking to go somewhere private, and having a door that only opens into the private room.

sections.title: What Servers and Providers Must Do
sections.content:
MSPs that support POP, IMAP or Message Submission MUST support TLS access for them, SHOULD provide Implicit TLS instances, and SHOULD also offer STARTTLS in the near term for legacy clients. Servers MUST support TLS 1.2 or later and SHOULD implement the ciphersuites recommended in RFC 7525. MSPs still supporting SSL 2.x, SSL 3.0 or TLS 1.0 SHOULD move users to TLS 1.1 or later.

Cleartext should be deprecated as soon as practicable, possibly in stages, and eventually disabled or limited to legacy systems. Once a user may no longer authenticate in cleartext, the server MUST NOT reveal over a cleartext channel whether the credentials were valid. Users whose passwords were sent in cleartext SHOULD be required to change them, since some compromise should be assumed. MSPs MUST maintain valid server certificates.

Servers that accept mail over TLS SHOULD record the ciphersuite in the Received header with a new tls clause, optionally followed by a group clause naming the Diffie-Hellman group.
sections.eli5: Mail companies must lock their doors properly, keep the locks up to date, and then stop leaving the old unlocked door open.

sections.title: DNS Records and Account Discovery
sections.content:
MSPs SHOULD advertise their servers with DNS SRV records as described in RFC 6186, listing servers that support Implicit TLS in preference to those that use STARTTLS or cleartext. RFC 8314 updates RFC 6186 by changing the preference rules and adding a service label _submissions._tcp for submission with Implicit TLS.

DNS records that help clients SHOULD be signed with DNSSEC when the parent zone allows it. MSPs SHOULD publish TLSA records as an extra trust anchor, but MUST NOT advertise them unless they are DNSSEC-signed. MX records for inbound mail are recommended to be DNSSEC-signed too, though inbound mail is out of scope.

When an MUA configures an account from SRV records, it SHOULD verify that the records are DNSSEC-signed or that the target name matches the queried domain, and it MUST NOT consult SRV records on every connection unless they are validly signed.
sections.eli5: A provider can publish a signed sign saying where its secure mail doors are, and mail apps can read the sign when you set up an account.

sections.title: What Mail Clients Must Do
sections.content:
MUAs MUST implement TLS 1.2 or later. By default they SHOULD require a minimum level of confidentiality per account. For new accounts that minimum MUST require successful validation of the server certificate and SHOULD require TLS 1.1 or greater. A client with such a requirement MUST NOT do anything beyond capability discovery, or STARTTLS, until the minimum is met.

Users may be allowed to turn the requirement off, but the MUA MUST warn that passwords and messages will not be private. MUAs SHOULD NOT let users easily click through a failed connection, because users who click through often do so without understanding the risk and can become conditioned to it. An MUA MUST NOT test a configuration by sending credentials unless the minimum confidentiality level has been met, and it SHOULD detect when TLS becomes available and offer to upgrade.

MUAs MUST validate server certificates per RFC 7817 and PKIX, and MAY also use DANE. A lock icon or similar indicator, if shown, MUST NOT appear for a connection lacking at least TLS 1.1 with certificate verification.
sections.eli5: A mail app should refuse to hand over your password unless the connection is properly private, and should not let you wave away the warning too easily.

sections.title: Certificate Pinning and Client Certificates
sections.content:
If a server certificate fails validation during account setup, an MUA MAY offer certificate pinning, a persistent binding between that certificate and the saved hostname. It MUST NOT be offered after a validation failure on an existing account, MUST NOT apply to other accounts, and MUST be undoable. A pinned connection is exposed to a man-in-the-middle attack at setup time, so it does not count as meeting the minimum confidentiality level.

Client certificate authentication on the Implicit TLS port is optional. A server MUST NOT request a client certificate unless it can map one to an authorization identity, and a client MUST NOT offer one unless the server requests it and the client is authorized to use it with that account. Both sides MUST use the SASL EXTERNAL mechanism when this is done.
sections.eli5: Pinning is like deciding to trust one stranger's ID card once, which is risky if the stranger was lying that first time.

sections.title: Port Registrations
sections.content:
IANA updated the registrations for pop3s (TCP 995) and imaps (TCP 993), and assigned an alternate usage of TCP port 465 as submissions. The RFC calls the last one a one-time procedural exception that does not set a precedent.

The history explains why. Port 465 was briefly registered as smtps, then revoked and reassigned. Some widely deployed mail software nonetheless used it for submission by default. Registering a different port would have left either an inaccurate registry or harmful confusion, so the authors preferred a registry "wart" documenting real use. IANA also added the tls and group clauses for Received fields.
sections.eli5: A mailbox number got reused for two things by accident, so the official list now admits both uses instead of pretending only one exists.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Limits
sections.content:
The whole document is about security. It targets threats outside the email system, such as network snooping and interception, and is not meant to stop active attackers who have compromised provider systems. Antivirus and antispam proxies that intercept SMTP at the application layer can interfere with these requirements, and such a service is considered compatible only if all its IMAP, POP and SMTP software complies.

With TLS 1.2 and earlier, a client certificate reveals the user's identity to anyone reading packets on the path, so it should be presented only with explicit authorization. TLS 1.3 appears to reduce the risk somewhat. Appendix A also records the authors' view that STARTTLS is a less secure architecture, citing a command injection vulnerability that several implementers made independently.
sections.eli5: Sealing the envelope protects against people watching the road, but not against a thief already inside the post office.
